text: Which keyword declares a value that is fixed at compile time and cannot be changed afterward?
options: readonly
const
static
sealed
hint: Think of the keyword used for compile-time constants such as const int Max = 10;.
explanation: const values are substituted at compile time and must be initialized with a constant expression. readonly fields can be assigned at declaration or in a constructor, so they are runtime constants. static and sealed do not make a value immutable.

text: What is the default value of an uninitialized bool field in a class?
options: false
true
null
It is a compile error to leave it uninitialized
hint: Fields are zero-initialized by the runtime.
explanation: Class fields are automatically set to their default value, which is false for bool. bool is a value type so it cannot be null, and fields (unlike locals) do not need definite assignment.

text: Which statement about System.String is true?
options: It is a mutable value type
It is a mutable reference type
It is an immutable reference type
It is an immutable value type
hint: Methods such as Replace or ToUpper return something new.
explanation: string is a reference type whose instances cannot be modified after creation; operations return new strings. It is not a value type, and it is not mutable (that is StringBuilder's role).

text: Which of the following collection types can grow and shrink dynamically?
options: int[]
string
Span<int>
List<int>
hint: Arrays have a fixed length once created.
explanation: List<T> manages a resizable internal array and offers Add/Remove. Arrays and Span<T> have a fixed length, and string is an immutable sequence of chars.

text: What is the main purpose of Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.TryGetValue?
options: To look up a key without throwing an exception when it is missing
To add a key only if it is absent
To remove a key and return its value
To copy all keys into a list
hint: It returns a bool.
explanation: TryGetValue returns false and a default value when the key is missing, avoiding the KeyNotFoundException that the indexer would throw. Adding is done by Add/TryAdd and removal by Remove.

text: Which of the following can a C# class do? (Select all that apply.)
options: Inherit directly from two base classes
Inherit from one base class
Inherit from a struct
Implement multiple interfaces
hint: C# allows single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation.
explanation: A class has exactly one base class (System.Object by default) and may implement any number of interfaces. Multiple class inheritance is not supported, and structs cannot be base types.

text: What does the await keyword do inside an async method?
options: Blocks the current thread until the task completes
Starts a new thread for the awaited call
Asynchronously suspends the method until the awaited task completes, without blocking the thread
Converts the method to run synchronously
hint: The thread is freed to do other work in the meantime.
explanation: await registers the rest of the method as a continuation and returns control to the caller if the task is not complete. It does not block and does not itself create a thread.

text: Which return type should an async method normally use when it produces no value?
options: void
Task
bool
object
hint: The caller must be able to await it and observe exceptions.
explanation: Task lets callers await the method and observe exceptions. async void is reserved for event handlers because errors cannot be caught by the caller. bool and object imply a result that is not produced.

text: Which namespace must be imported to use LINQ extension methods such as Where and Select on collections?
options: System.Linq
System.Collections.Generic
System.Data
System.Text
hint: The namespace is named after the feature.
explanation: Enumerable extension methods like Where and Select live in System.Linq. System.Collections.Generic holds the collection types, but not these query operators.

text: What do C# record types provide by default?
options: Reference equality only
Mandatory immutability of all fields
Value-based equality and a generated ToString
Automatic database mapping
hint: Two records with the same data compare as equal.
explanation: Records generate Equals/GetHashCode based on member values and a ToString that prints them. They are not forced to be immutable (positional properties are init-only, but you can add mutable ones) and have nothing to do with databases.

text: With nullable reference types enabled, what does the declaration string? name mean?
options: name is a value type
name may hold null
name can never be assigned
name is lazily evaluated
hint: The question mark is an annotation about null.
explanation: string? tells the compiler that null is an expected value, so it warns on unchecked dereference. Without the ? the compiler treats the variable as non-null. It does not change the runtime type.

text: In ASP.NET Core dependency injection, which lifetime creates a new instance every time the service is requested?
options: Singleton
Scoped
Static
Transient
hint: The name suggests a short-lived instance.
explanation: Transient services are created each time they are resolved. Singleton gives one instance per container and Scoped one per scope (usually per HTTP request). Static is not a DI lifetime.

text: Which file is the default place for application configuration settings in an ASP.NET Core project?
options: appsettings.json
web.xml
Startup.config
launch.cfg
hint: It is a JSON file loaded by the default host builder.
explanation: The default host loads appsettings.json plus appsettings.{Environment}.json. The other names are not used by default.

text: What does app.MapGet("/hello", () => "Hi") do in a minimal API?
options: Registers a handler for HTTP POST requests to /hello
Registers a middleware that runs for every request
Registers a handler for HTTP GET requests to /hello
Reads a value from configuration
hint: Match the verb in the method name.
explanation: MapGet creates an endpoint that responds to GET requests on the given route pattern. Handlers for POST use MapPost, and middleware is registered with Use/Run.

text: In EF Core, what does a DbContext represent?
options: A single table row
A session with the database used to query and save entities
A SQL Server login
A database migration
hint: It combines the unit of work and repository ideas.
explanation: DbContext is the main class for interacting with the database: it tracks entities, runs queries and saves changes. A table row is an entity instance and a migration is a schema change script.

text: In EF Core, what does a DbSet<TEntity> property on a DbContext represent?
options: A connection string
A transaction
A queryable collection of entities of type TEntity, usually mapped to a table
A migration history
hint: You write context.Customers.Where(...) using it.
explanation: DbSet<T> exposes the set of entities for querying and adding/removing. It is not a connection or transaction, although it is used within them.

text: When does the code in a finally block run?
options: Only when an exception is thrown
Only when no exception is thrown
Only if there is a catch block
Whether or not an exception occurs
hint: It is used for cleanup.
explanation: finally runs after the try (and any catch) completes, regardless of whether an exception was thrown. It does not require a catch block; try/finally is valid on its own.

text: What does the delegate type Func<int, string> represent?
options: A method that takes an int and returns a string
A method that takes a string and returns an int
A method that takes an int and returns nothing
A property of type int
hint: In Func, the last type argument is the return type.
explanation: Func<TArg, TResult> has the result type last, so this is int -> string. A method returning nothing would be Action<int>.

text: What does the constraint where T : class mean on a generic type parameter?
options: T must be a struct
T must be a reference type
T must be a class declared in the same assembly
T must be abstract
hint: It limits the kind of types allowed, not their location.
explanation: where T : class restricts T to reference types (classes, interfaces, delegates, arrays). Value types use where T : struct. It says nothing about assembly or being abstract.

text: Which keyword does a derived class use to replace the implementation of a virtual method of its base class?
options: new
sealed
override
abstract
hint: The base method must be marked virtual, abstract or override.
explanation: override provides a new implementation for a virtual member and participates in polymorphic dispatch. new merely hides the member, and sealed/abstract serve other purposes.

text: What does marking a class as sealed do?
options: Prevents other classes from inheriting from it
Prevents creating instances of it
Makes all its members static
Makes it thread-safe
hint: Think of closing the inheritance chain.
explanation: A sealed class cannot be used as a base class. It can still be instantiated (that is what abstract prevents) and its members are unaffected.

text: What is true about a local variable declared with var?
options: Its type is determined at run time
It can hold any type and change type later
It must be a reference type
Its type is inferred by the compiler at compile time
hint: C# remains statically typed.
explanation: var asks the compiler to infer the static type from the initializer, so the variable has a fixed type afterward. It is not dynamic and works for value types too.

text: What is the output of this string interpolation example?
options: x = {x}
x = x
hint: The $ prefix evaluates expressions inside braces.
explanation: String interpolation replaces {x} with the value of the variable, so the output is x = 5. Without the $ prefix the braces would be printed literally.
code:
int x = 5;
Console.WriteLine($"x = {x}");

text: What is printed by this integer arithmetic?
hint: Both operands are int.
explanation: Integer division truncates, so 10 / 4 is 2, and 10 % 4 is the remainder 2. Concatenation with a string yields "2 2". 2.5 would need a double operand.
code: Console.WriteLine(10 / 4 + " " + 10 % 4);

text: What is printed when the ?? operator is applied to a null string?
options: (an empty line)
null
none
It throws NullReferenceException
hint: The ?? operator supplies a fallback for null.
explanation: The null-coalescing operator returns the right operand when the left one is null, so "none" is printed. Console.WriteLine(null string) would print an empty line, but that is not what happens here.
code:
string s = null;
Console.WriteLine(s ?? "none");

text: What does this Where/Select pipeline print?
hint: Where filters first, then Select transforms.
explanation: Where keeps the even numbers 2 and 4, and Select squares them to 4 and 16. The result is joined as 4,16. 2,4 would be the filter alone.
code:
var r = new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).Select(n => n * n);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", r));

text: Which of the following are value types in C#? (Select all that apply.)
options: int
List<int>
DateTime
string
hint: Value types include primitives and structs.
explanation: int and DateTime are structs and therefore value types. string and List<int> are classes (reference types), even though string has value-like equality.

text: Which of the following are valid C# access modifiers? (Select all that apply.)
options: public
internal
package
protected
friend
hint: friend and package belong to other languages.
explanation: public, internal and protected are all C# access modifiers (along with private, protected internal and private protected). friend is C++/VB and package is Java.

text: Which of the following are service lifetimes supported by the built-in ASP.NET Core DI container? (Select all that apply.)
options: Singleton
Transient
Scoped
Static
hint: There are exactly three lifetimes.
explanation: The built-in container supports Singleton, Scoped and Transient. Static is a C# modifier but not a DI lifetime.

text: Which of these are real endpoint-mapping methods for minimal APIs? (Select all that apply.)
options: MapGet
MapFetch
MapPost
MapDelete
hint: They mirror HTTP verbs.
explanation: MapGet, MapPost, MapPut, MapDelete and MapPatch exist for the corresponding HTTP verbs. MapFetch is not a method; fetch is a JavaScript API.

text: Why is async void generally discouraged outside of event handlers?
options: It runs on a dedicated thread
Callers cannot await it, and exceptions thrown inside cannot be caught by the caller
It cannot contain await expressions
It always executes synchronously
hint: Consider how a caller can observe completion or failure.
explanation: An async void method gives the caller no Task, so completion cannot be awaited and unhandled exceptions are raised on the synchronization context, often crashing the process. It can contain await and does not use a special thread.

text: Two tasks passed to await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2) both fault with different exceptions. What does the await expression throw?
options: An AggregateException containing both
Only the first exception; the others are available on the WhenAll task's Exception property
Nothing, because WhenAll swallows exceptions
A TaskCanceledException
hint: await unwraps AggregateException.
explanation: await rethrows only the first inner exception for convenience. The task returned by WhenAll still exposes all exceptions through its Exception (AggregateException) property. Exceptions are not swallowed.

text: Which problems can result from blocking on an asynchronous operation with task.Result or task.Wait()? (Select all that apply.)
options: Deadlocks in environments that have a synchronization context
Thread-pool threads are tied up, which can cause starvation under load
Exceptions are wrapped in an AggregateException
The awaited task is executed twice
hint: Think about threads, exceptions and contexts.
explanation: Blocking holds a thread while waiting, so many concurrent requests can starve the pool. Result/Wait wrap failures in AggregateException, and where a SynchronizationContext exists (UI apps, classic ASP.NET) the continuation may need the blocked thread, causing a deadlock. The task is never run twice.

text: What does this program print?
options: A B C
B C A
B A C
A C B
hint: An async method runs synchronously until its first incomplete await.
explanation: DoAsync starts running immediately on the calling thread and prints B, then reaches the await on Task.Delay and returns an incomplete task. The caller prints A, then awaits and C is printed after the delay.

text: Which statements about cancellation with CancellationToken are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Task.Delay(1000, token) completes as canceled if the token is canceled during the delay
Cancellation is cooperative: the code must observe the token
Calling Cancel() immediately aborts the running thread
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() throws OperationCanceledException when cancellation was requested
hint: Cancel() only sets a flag and runs callbacks.
explanation: Cancellation never forcibly aborts a thread; code must check the token or pass it to APIs that do. ThrowIfCancellationRequested throws OperationCanceledException, and Task.Delay with a token ends in the canceled state (awaiting it throws TaskCanceledException, a subclass).

text: Each call to FetchAsync takes about one second and the three calls are independent. About how long does this loop take?
options: About 1 second, because await runs them in parallel
About 3 seconds, because each call is awaited before the next starts
About 0 seconds, because nothing is awaited
It deadlocks
hint: Look at where the await is placed.
explanation: Awaiting inside the loop starts the next call only after the previous one finishes, so the calls run sequentially (~3 s). To run them concurrently you would start all tasks first and then await Task.WhenAll.

text: What does this deferred-execution query print?
options: It throws InvalidOperationException
hint: The query is not executed when it is defined.
explanation: Where is deferred, so the query runs when Count() is called, after 4 was added. The elements greater than 1 are 2, 3 and 4, giving 3. Modifying the list does not throw here because it is not being enumerated at that time.

text: For the sequence { 1, 2 }, which calls throw InvalidOperationException? (Select all that apply.)
options: seq.Single()
seq.SingleOrDefault()
seq.First()
seq.FirstOrDefault()
hint: Single variants require at most one match.
explanation: Single and SingleOrDefault throw when more than one element exists (SingleOrDefault only tolerates zero). First and FirstOrDefault simply return the first element.

text: What does this SelectMany query print?
options: a b|c
ab|c
a|b|c
System.String[]
hint: SelectMany flattens the inner sequences.
explanation: Each string is split into an array, and SelectMany flattens the arrays into a single sequence a, b, c. Select would yield two arrays instead.
code:
var r = new[] { "a b", "c" }.SelectMany(s => s.Split(' '));
Console.WriteLine(string.Join("|", r));

text: What does this code print (one item per line)?
options: a:2 then b:1
a:1 then b:1
a:2, a:2 then b:1
hint: GroupBy groups by the key selector result.
explanation: GroupBy groups by first character: apple and avocado share 'a' (count 2) and banana is alone under 'b'. Groups appear in order of first occurrence.

text: What does this OrderBy query print?
options: bb,cc,a,d
d,a,cc,bb
a,bb,cc,d
a,d,bb,cc
hint: OrderBy is a stable sort.
explanation: Items are ordered by length ascending; OrderBy is stable, so equal-length items keep their original relative order (a before d, bb before cc).
code:
var r = new[] { "bb", "a", "cc", "d" }.OrderBy(s => s.Length);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", r));

text: What does this dictionary indexer code print?
options: It throws ArgumentException
hint: The indexer setter overwrites existing keys.
explanation: Assigning through the indexer adds or replaces, so the dictionary holds one entry with value 2. Only Add would throw ArgumentException for a duplicate key.

text: What happens if you call list.Remove(x) inside a foreach over the same List<T>?
options: The item is removed and enumeration continues safely
The next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException because the collection was modified
The loop silently stops
A compile-time error occurs
hint: List<T> tracks a version number.
explanation: List<T>'s enumerator detects structural modification and throws InvalidOperationException on the next iteration. Iterate over a copy or use RemoveAll to avoid this.

text: Which of these types are safe for concurrent reads and writes from multiple threads without external locking? (Select all that apply.)
options: List<T>
ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>
ConcurrentQueue<T>
Dictionary<TKey,TValue>
hint: Look for the Concurrent prefix.
explanation: The collections in System.Collections.Concurrent are designed for thread-safe use. List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> are not safe for concurrent writes.

text: What does this virtual/override call print?
options: A
AB
It does not compile
B
hint: Virtual dispatch uses the runtime type.
explanation: N is virtual and overridden, so the call through an A reference runs B's implementation, based on the object's runtime type.

text: What does this method-hiding example print?
options: A
B
AB
It does not compile
hint: The new modifier hides rather than overrides.
explanation: The method is not virtual, and new only hides the base member for callers using B. Because the variable's static type is A, A.N() is bound at compile time and returns "A".

text: Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: An abstract class can declare instance fields and constructors
A class can implement several interfaces
An abstract class can be instantiated directly with new
An interface can declare instance fields
hint: Abstract means it needs a derived class.
explanation: Abstract classes can hold state and constructors (called by derived classes) and a class can implement many interfaces. Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly, and interfaces cannot declare instance fields.

text: What does this struct copy example print?
options: It does not compile
hint: Structs are copied on assignment.
explanation: struct is a value type, so var b = a copies the data and changing b.X does not affect a. With a class both variables would reference the same object and the output would be 2.

text: What does the new() constraint on a type parameter allow?
options: Calling any constructor with arguments
Creating an instance with new T(), because T must have a public parameterless constructor
Restricting T to value types
Allowing T to be null
hint: Only the parameterless form is expressible.
explanation: where T : new() guarantees a public parameterless constructor so the generic code can write new T(). Constructors with arguments cannot be constrained this way.

text: What does this generic Max call print?
options: apple
It does not compile
It throws ArgumentException
banana
hint: string implements IComparable<string>.
explanation: string satisfies IComparable<string>, T is inferred as string, and "apple".CompareTo("banana") is negative so b is returned.

text: Which of these are valid generic constraints in C#? (Select all that apply.)
options: where T : unmanaged
where T : class
where T : sealed
where T : struct
hint: Constraints describe capabilities, not modifiers.
explanation: struct, class and unmanaged are valid constraints. sealed is a class modifier, not a constraint.

text: What does this record equality code print?
options: True True
False False
True False
False True
hint: Record equality compares members, not references.
explanation: Records generate value-based == and Equals, so a == b is True, but they are still distinct objects so ReferenceEquals returns False.

text: What does this with-expression code print?
hint: A with-expression creates a copy.
explanation: with creates a new record that is a copy of the original with the listed properties changed, leaving the original untouched, so a.Age is 1 and b.Age is 2.

text: For the declaration record P(string Name);, which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: ToString prints the member values
Name is an init-only property, so it cannot be assigned after construction
Equals compares the Name values
P is a value type
hint: A plain record is a class.
explanation: A positional record class gets value equality, a printing ToString and init-only properties. A record without struct is a reference type; record struct would be the value type.

text: What is the effect of enabling nullable reference types in a project?
options: Reference types can no longer hold null at run time
The compiler produces nullability warnings; no runtime checks are added
All strings become Nullable<string>
Null dereferences throw a different exception
hint: It is a static analysis feature.
explanation: Nullable reference types are annotations used by compiler flow analysis to warn about possible null dereferences. They do not change runtime behavior and string? is not Nullable<string>.

text: What does the null-forgiving operator (!) do in expressions like user!.Name?
options: Throws if user is null
Suppresses the compiler's nullable warning without any runtime null check
Converts null to an empty object
Makes user non-nullable at run time
hint: It only silences the compiler.
explanation: The ! operator tells the compiler to treat the expression as non-null; it emits no check, so a null value still causes NullReferenceException at the dereference.

text: What does this null-conditional code print?
options: null
It throws NullReferenceException
hint: ?. short-circuits to null.
explanation: s?.Length evaluates to a null int?, and ?? supplies -1. No exception occurs because of the null-conditional operator.

text: What does this switch expression print?
options: intbignull
intintnull
bigbignull
othersbigother
hint: Switch expression arms are evaluated top to bottom.
explanation: 5 is an int but fails the guard, so it matches the int arm; 50 matches the guarded arm and gives big; null matches the null arm.

text: What does this property pattern code print?
options: True
False
It does not compile
It throws InvalidCastException
hint: A property pattern tests type and members together.
explanation: o is P { Age: >= 18 } checks that o is a P and that its Age satisfies the relational pattern. The age is 20, so the result is True.

text: What happens when a switch expression receives a value that none of its arms match and there is no discard arm?
options: It returns default
It throws a SwitchExpressionException at run time
It falls through to the next arm
It silently returns null
hint: Switch expressions must produce a value.
explanation: The compiler may warn the switch is not exhaustive, and if no arm matches at run time a SwitchExpressionException is thrown. There is no fall-through or default result.

text: Why does the order of middleware registration in Program.cs matter?
options: Middleware executes in the order registered for requests, and in reverse order for responses
Middleware always executes alphabetically
Only the last registered middleware runs
Order matters only in Production
hint: It forms a pipeline.
explanation: Each middleware decides whether to call the next one, and code after await next() runs on the way back. For example UseAuthentication must precede UseAuthorization.

text: What is the order of the console output for one request to this pipeline?
options: 1 in, handler, 1 out
handler, 1 in, 1 out
1 in, 1 out, handler
1 in, handler
hint: Code after next() runs after later middleware returns.
explanation: The Use middleware prints 1 in, calls next (reaching the terminal Run handler which prints handler), then resumes and prints 1 out.

text: Which of the following are valid ways to implement middleware? (Select all that apply.)
options: A class with a RequestDelegate constructor parameter and an Invoke/InvokeAsync(HttpContext) method
A class decorated with a [Middleware] attribute
Inline with app.Use(async (ctx, next) => ...)
A class implementing IMiddleware
hint: No special attribute exists for middleware.
explanation: Inline delegates, conventional middleware classes and IMiddleware implementations are all supported. There is no [Middleware] attribute.

text: In conventional (convention-based) middleware, where should you inject a scoped service such as a DbContext?
options: In the constructor
As a parameter of the InvokeAsync method
In a static field
It cannot be injected
hint: The middleware instance is created once at startup.
explanation: Conventional middleware is constructed once, so constructor dependencies behave as singletons. Scoped services should be taken as InvokeAsync parameters, which are resolved per request.

text: Where in the pipeline should exception-handling middleware such as UseExceptionHandler normally be placed?
options: As early as possible so it wraps later middleware
After UseEndpoints
Last, after all other middleware
It must be inside every controller
hint: It can only catch exceptions from middleware after it.
explanation: Middleware wraps the ones registered after it, so the exception handler should be registered first to catch their exceptions.

text: Which statement about app.Run(...) is correct?
options: It starts the web host
It adds terminal middleware that does not call the next delegate
It runs a handler only for POST requests
It runs after the response is sent
hint: Compare with app.Use.
explanation: app.Run registers a terminal middleware, with no next parameter. app.Run() with no arguments starts the host, which is a different overload.

text: Which are benefits of using IHttpClientFactory instead of creating a new HttpClient for every request? (Select all that apply.)
options: Handlers are recycled periodically so DNS changes are picked up
Handlers are pooled, which avoids socket exhaustion
It is required to call HTTPS endpoints
HTTP calls become synchronous
hint: Think about the HttpMessageHandler lifetime.
explanation: Creating many HttpClient instances can exhaust sockets, while a single static one can hold stale DNS. The factory manages pooled handlers with periodic recycling. It does not change sync behavior and HTTPS works without it.

text: By default in ASP.NET Core, which configuration source has the highest precedence when the same key is defined in several places?
options: appsettings.json
appsettings.Development.json
Environment variables
Command-line arguments
hint: Later sources override earlier ones.
explanation: The default order is appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (in Development), environment variables, then command-line arguments, and later providers win.

text: A singleton service must see updated settings after appsettings.json changes without restarting the app. Which options type is appropriate?
options: IOptions<T>
IOptionsSnapshot<T>
IOptionsMonitor<T>
A static field
hint: Snapshot is scoped, so it cannot be injected into a singleton.
explanation: IOptionsMonitor<T> is a singleton that gives current values and change notifications. IOptions<T> is computed once, and IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so it cannot be injected into singletons.

text: How is the configuration key Logging:LogLevel:Default set through an environment variable?
options: Logging:LogLevel:Default always works on every OS
Logging__LogLevel__Default
Logging.LogLevel.Default
LOGGING-LOGLEVEL-DEFAULT
hint: Colons are not portable in environment variable names.
explanation: A double underscore is translated into the configuration key separator by the environment variables provider. The colon form works only on some platforms.

text: Why is logger.LogInformation("User {UserId} logged in", id) preferred over logger.LogInformation($"User {id} logged in")?
options: Interpolation does not compile
The message template keeps UserId as a structured property and avoids formatting work when the level is disabled
Interpolation is slower only on Linux
The template version writes to a file
hint: Think of structured logging sinks.
explanation: Named placeholders let providers capture values as structured data and format lazily. An interpolated string is built eagerly and loses the structure. Both compile.

text: The minimum log level is Warning. Which of these calls produce output? (Select all that apply.)
options: LogDebug
LogWarning
LogError
LogInformation
hint: Levels order: Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical.
explanation: Only messages at or above the minimum level are written, so Warning and Error are output. Information and Debug are lower.

text: What is the correct way to log an exception with its stack trace using ILogger?
options: logger.LogError(ex.Message)
logger.LogError(ex, "Failed to process order {OrderId}", id)
logger.LogError("Failed: " + ex.ToString().Length)
Console.WriteLine(ex)
hint: Pass the exception as the first argument.
explanation: The overload taking Exception first lets providers record the full exception and details. Logging only Message loses the stack trace and Console.WriteLine bypasses the logging system.

text: In app.MapGet("/users/{id}", (int id) => ...), where does id come from?
options: The route value
The request body
A header
A DI service
hint: The name matches a route template parameter.
explanation: A simple parameter whose name matches a route template segment is bound from the route. Complex types on POST are bound from the body and services from DI.

text: In app.MapPost("/items", (Item item) => ...), where Item is a class, how is item bound?
options: From the JSON request body
From the query string
From a route value
From a cookie
hint: Complex types are read from the body by default.
explanation: For POST/PUT/PATCH handlers, a complex type parameter that is not a registered service is bound from the JSON body. Use [FromQuery] etc. to override.

text: A singleton service takes a scoped service in its constructor. What happens when scope validation is enabled (default in Development)?
options: It works and the scoped service is created per request
The container throws InvalidOperationException when resolving
The singleton becomes scoped
The scoped service becomes transient
hint: The singleton would capture a short-lived dependency.
explanation: Injecting a scoped service into a singleton is a captive dependency, as the scoped instance would live as long as the singleton. Scope validation detects it and throws.

text: What does this scoped-lifetime code print?
options: True True
False True
False False
True False
hint: Scoped means one instance per scope.
explanation: Within the same scope the same instance is returned (a == b), but a different scope gets its own instance, so a == c is False.

text: IFoo is registered twice: AddTransient<IFoo, A>() then AddTransient<IFoo, B>(). What do GetRequiredService<IFoo>() and GetServices<IFoo>() return?
options: Error for both calls because of ambiguity
B for the single resolution; both A and B for the collection
A for the single resolution; only B for the collection
Both return a list of A and B
hint: Later registrations override earlier ones for single resolution.
explanation: The last registration wins for a single resolve, while resolving IEnumerable<IFoo> returns all registrations in order. There is no ambiguity error.

text: Which statements about service disposal in the built-in container are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Instances passed to AddSingleton(instance) are not disposed by the container
IDisposable services created by the container are disposed when their scope or the provider is disposed
Singleton services are disposed at the end of each request
The container never disposes anything
hint: Ownership matters: who created the object?
explanation: The container disposes what it creates, at the end of its owning scope or provider. Instances you supply yourself are left to you. Singletons live until the root provider is disposed.

text: Which techniques reduce overhead for a read-only query whose results will not be modified? (Select all that apply.)
options: Projecting only the needed columns with Select()
Calling SaveChanges() after the query
AsNoTracking()
Calling Include() for every navigation property
hint: Avoid tracking and avoid loading unneeded data.
explanation: AsNoTracking skips change tracking and identity resolution, and a projection fetches only the columns you need (projected non-entity results are not tracked at all). Loading every navigation does more work, and SaveChanges is irrelevant to reading.

text: What is the N+1 query problem in EF Core?
options: One query to load the parent entities, plus one additional query per parent to load related data
Running N queries in one transaction
Using more than one DbContext
Having N tables with one foreign key
hint: Related data is loaded lazily in a loop.
explanation: Iterating over parents and touching a navigation (e.g. with lazy loading) issues extra queries per item. Using Include or a projection loads everything in a few queries.

text: After loading a User entity and changing only its Name property, SaveChangesAsync is called. What SQL does EF Core generate?
options: An INSERT of the whole entity
An UPDATE that sets only the modified column(s)
A DELETE followed by an INSERT
No SQL because it only works with AsNoTracking
hint: The change tracker knows what changed.
explanation: Tracked entities have their property changes detected, and EF Core emits an UPDATE with only the modified columns. Tracking is what makes this possible; AsNoTracking would prevent it.

text: Which of these calls cause the query to be executed against the database immediately? (Select all that apply.)
options: Where(x => x.Active)
Select(x => x.Name)
CountAsync()
ToListAsync()
hint: Operators that return IQueryable are lazy.
explanation: ToListAsync and CountAsync materialize a result and run the query. Where and Select only compose a deferred IQueryable.

text: What is the default lifetime of a DbContext registered with AddDbContext, and why does it matter?
options: Scoped; a DbContext is not thread-safe and should not be shared across concurrent requests
Singleton; it caches data forever
Transient; a new one per call
Static; shared across the process
hint: Think of one unit of work per request.
explanation: AddDbContext registers it as scoped, so each request gets its own instance. DbContext is not thread-safe, so a singleton would break under concurrency.

text: A row has a rowversion/[Timestamp] concurrency token and another user updated it after you loaded it. What does SaveChanges do?
options: Silently overwrites the other user's change
Throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException
Merges the changes automatically
Rolls back the other user's update
hint: EF adds the token to the WHERE clause.
explanation: The UPDATE includes the original token in its WHERE clause, affects zero rows, and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. It does not merge or overwrite the other change.

text: What does this try/catch/finally code print?
options: TCE
TFCE
TCFE
TCF
hint: finally runs before control continues after the try statement.
explanation: T is written, the exception is caught (C), finally runs (F) and then execution continues after the try statement (E).

text: What does this event code print?
options: hi
HI
Nothing, because events need a null check
hiHI
hint: Both handlers are subscribed.
explanation: Invoke calls all subscribed handlers in subscription order, so hi followed by HI is printed. The null-conditional Invoke handles the case of no subscribers.

text: What does this closure-in-a-for-loop code print?
options: It throws
hint: How many i variables does a for loop create?
explanation: A for loop declares a single i shared by all closures, which has the value 3 once the loop ends, so 333 is printed. A foreach iteration variable is per-iteration.

text: What does this Substring and indexer code print?
options: bc
b
c
It does not compile
hint: string + char produces a string.
explanation: Substring(1, 1) is "b", and "abc"[2] is the char 'c'. Concatenating string and char gives "bc".
code: Console.WriteLine("abc".Substring(1, 1) + "abc"[2]);

text: Which restriction applies to Span<T>?
options: It can only hold reference types
It is a ref struct, so it cannot be a class field or be used across await in an async method
It always allocates on the heap
It can only be used with arrays
hint: It must live on the stack.
explanation: Span<T> is a ref struct restricted to the stack, so it cannot be stored in a class field, boxed or kept across an await. It can wrap arrays, stack memory and native memory and works with any T.

text: A lambda increments a captured local and is invoked twice. What is the local's value afterwards?
options: It does not compile because lambdas cannot modify captured locals
hint: The lambda captures the variable itself.
explanation: A closure captures the variable, not a copy of its value, so each call increments the same local. Lambdas are allowed to modify captured locals, so it does compile.

text: Lambdas are added to a list inside a for loop and invoked afterwards. What is the output?
options: It does not compile because i is modified after capture
hint: Think about how many variables the for loop declares.
explanation: A for loop declares a single loop variable shared by all iterations, and the lambdas capture that variable, not its value. By the time they run, i is 3. The 0 1 2 result would need a per-iteration copy such as 'int c = i;'.

text: Lambdas are added to a list inside a foreach loop and invoked afterwards. What is the output?
options: It does not compile because the foreach variable is read-only inside lambdas
hint: Compare how foreach declares its iteration variable with how for does.
explanation: Since C# 5 the foreach iteration variable is scoped inside the loop body, so each iteration gets a fresh variable that the lambda captures. Each action therefore remembers its own value. Capturing a for-loop counter behaves differently.

text: An element is added to the list after the Where query is defined. What is printed?
options: It throws InvalidOperationException because the list was modified
hint: When does Where actually look at the source list?
explanation: Where is lazy, so the query is evaluated when Count() enumerates it, after 4 has been added. The elements greater than 1 at that moment are 2, 3 and 4, giving 3. No exception occurs because the list is not modified during enumeration.

text: How many times is the Select lambda executed, and what is printed?
hint: Each ToList enumerates the query from scratch.
explanation: Select is deferred and not cached, so each ToList call re-runs the lambda for all three elements, giving 6. 3 would be correct only if results were memoized, and nothing is memoized in LINQ to Objects.

text: Which of these LINQ operators execute (enumerate the source) immediately when called, rather than deferring until the result is enumerated? (Select all that apply.)
options: ToList()
Where(...)
OrderBy(...)
Select(...)
Count()
hint: Think about which ones return a materialized value rather than a query.
explanation: ToList and Count produce a concrete result so they enumerate immediately. Where, Select and OrderBy return lazy sequences that do no work until enumerated.

text: A repository method is declared as below. How is the filter applied for a SQL provider?
options: It is translated to a SQL WHERE clause because the source is a DbSet
The whole Orders table is loaded and the filter runs in memory
EF Core throws because Where cannot accept a lambda on IEnumerable
Only the first matching row is loaded
hint: Look at the static type of the variable q.
explanation: Typing the variable as IEnumerable<Order> makes Where bind to Enumerable.Where, which takes a Func rather than an expression tree. The rest of the query becomes LINQ to Objects, so every row is fetched and filtered in memory. Keeping IQueryable would translate the predicate to SQL.
code:
IEnumerable<Order> q = db.Orders;
var big = q.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList();

text: What happens to the database when this code runs (default tracking behavior)?
options: A new row is inserted with the new price
The Price is updated because the entity was loaded from the context
Nothing is written: the entity is not tracked so SaveChanges sees no changes
SaveChangesAsync throws InvalidOperationException because the entity is untracked
hint: What does AsNoTracking skip?
explanation: AsNoTracking returns entities that are not attached to the change tracker, so modifying them is invisible to SaveChanges. No exception is thrown and nothing is inserted. You would need Update/Attach to persist the change.

text: With lazy-loading proxies enabled and Customer declared as a virtual navigation property, how many SQL queries does this code run for 50 orders?
hint: One query for the list plus one per navigation access.
explanation: ToList issues one query for the orders, and the first access to each o.Customer triggers a separate lazy-load query, giving 1 + N = 51 (fewer if customers repeat, since the context caches already loaded ones, but the worst case is 51). This is the classic N+1 problem, fixed with Include or a projection.
code:
foreach (var o in db.Orders.ToList())
    Console.WriteLine(o.Customer.Name);

text: A query includes two sibling collection navigations (Include(a => a.Orders).Include(a => a.Addresses)) and returns far more rows than expected, causing slow performance. Which approaches mitigate this cartesian explosion? (Select all that apply.)
options: Load each collection with a separate query
Use AsSplitQuery()
Use AsNoTracking()
Call ToList() before Include
hint: The problem is the single JOINed result set.
explanation: Multiplying child collections in one JOIN duplicates parent data; AsSplitQuery or manually separate queries avoid it. AsNoTracking affects tracking only, and calling ToList first would make Include unavailable on the in-memory list.

text: Which of these calls return entity instances that are tracked by the DbContext under default settings? (Select all that apply.)
options: db.Products.Select(p => new { p.Id, p.Name }).ToList()
db.Products.AsNoTracking().ToList()
db.Products.Find(1)
db.Products.ToList()
hint: Anonymous types are not entities.
explanation: ToList on a DbSet and Find both return tracked entities. AsNoTracking opts out, and a projection into an anonymous type yields no entity instances to track.

text: What is the value of p.Price printed at the end?
options: The old price: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker so p is stale
99, because EF Core refreshes tracked entities after ExecuteUpdate
It throws because p is tracked
hint: Does set-based SQL know about objects already in memory?
explanation: ExecuteUpdateAsync issues a direct UPDATE statement and does not touch tracked entities, so p keeps the value read earlier. The database has 99, but the in-memory object is stale until reloaded.

text: An entity has a [Timestamp] byte[] RowVersion property. Two users load the same row and both save changes. What happens to the second SaveChanges?
options: The second save silently overwrites the first
It throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException because the UPDATE matched 0 rows
It throws only when both users edit the same column
EF Core automatically merges both changes
hint: The RowVersion is part of the UPDATE's WHERE clause.
explanation: EF Core adds the original RowVersion to the WHERE clause, so after the first save changes the version, the second UPDATE affects zero rows and EF raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException. It does not compare columns individually or merge changes.

text: What is the result of running this code with a single DbContext instance?
options: A DbUpdateException is raised
Both counts run in parallel and complete normally
InvalidOperationException because a second operation was started on the context before the first completed
The second query is automatically queued by the context
hint: Is DbContext thread-safe?
explanation: DbContext does not support multiple concurrent operations; EF Core detects this and throws InvalidOperationException. It does not queue requests. Use separate contexts (for example from IDbContextFactory) for parallel queries.

text: This method is called from a WinForms button click handler (UI thread with a SynchronizationContext). What happens?
options: It throws InvalidOperationException for cross-thread access
It returns null
It returns "x" after about 100 ms
It deadlocks
hint: Who is blocked, and where does the continuation want to run?
explanation: The UI thread blocks on .Result while the continuation after await Task.Delay needs to resume on that same UI thread, so neither can proceed. Using await up the call chain or ConfigureAwait(false) inside the helper avoids it.

text: Which statements about async void methods are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: An exception thrown from one cannot be caught by a try/catch around the call
Callers can await them to observe completion
An unhandled exception in one can crash the process (for example in a console app)
They are the recommended way to start general fire-and-forget work
hint: There is no Task to carry the failure.
explanation: async void has no Task, so exceptions are raised on the captured context or thread pool, bypassing the caller's catch and potentially terminating the process. It is meant for event handlers only, and it cannot be awaited.

text: Which statements about Task.WhenAll are correct when several of the tasks fault? (Select all that apply.)
options: It cancels the remaining tasks as soon as one faults
It completes as soon as the first task faults
All exceptions are available in whenAllTask.Exception.InnerExceptions
await on the WhenAll task rethrows only the first exception
hint: WhenAll waits for everyone.
explanation: WhenAll completes only after all tasks finish, aggregating failures; await unwraps and rethrows just the first, and the full set lives in the AggregateException. It never cancels the other tasks.

text: What is wrong with this method?
options: The reader is disposed before the returned task completes, so the read can fail with ObjectDisposedException
It does not compile because async is missing
ReadToEndAsync cannot be used with using var
Nothing: ReadToEndAsync completes before the method returns
hint: When does the using scope end relative to the task?
explanation: Without async/await the method returns the Task immediately, the using scope ends and disposes the reader while the read is still in flight. Making the method async and awaiting inside the using fixes it.

text: Which statements about ConfigureAwait(false) are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It forces the awaited operation to run on a thread-pool thread
In ASP.NET Core, omitting it in application code does not cause the classic sync-context deadlock
Code after the await may run without the captured SynchronizationContext
It suppresses exceptions from the awaited task
hint: It controls only where the continuation resumes.
explanation: ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so blocking there does not deadlock in the classic way, and ConfigureAwait(false) simply says the continuation need not resume on the captured context. It does not change where the awaited operation itself runs and does not touch exceptions.

text: Which statements about ValueTask<T> are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Awaiting a ValueTask once directly is a valid usage
Calling GetAwaiter().GetResult() on an incomplete ValueTask is a supported way to block
Awaiting the same ValueTask instance twice is not supported
Calling AsTask() once gives a Task that can be awaited multiple times
hint: A ValueTask may wrap a reusable pooled source.
explanation: A ValueTask must be consumed once; converting with AsTask gives a normal reusable Task. Blocking on an incomplete ValueTask via GetResult is unsupported.

text: What does this code print?
options: It throws InvalidOperationException from the call F()
after caught
caught
after, then an unhandled exception
hint: Where does an async method store an exception thrown before its first await?
explanation: In an async method, exceptions are captured in the returned Task, even when thrown before any await, so F() returns a faulted task. 'after' is printed first and await t then throws, which is caught.

text: What is the main problem with this code?
options: It deadlocks on the thread pool
Parallel.ForEach cannot take a lambda
The async lambda becomes async void, so Parallel.ForEach returns before the work finishes and exceptions are lost
The items are processed sequentially
hint: Which delegate type does Parallel.ForEach expect?
explanation: Parallel.ForEach takes an Action<T>, so the async lambda is compiled as async void and is not awaited. The loop returns when the lambdas hit their first await. Parallel.ForEachAsync or Task.WhenAll should be used.
code:
Parallel.ForEach(items, async item => await ProcessAsync(item));
Console.WriteLine("done");

text: A singleton service takes a scoped service in its constructor. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: With validation off, the scoped instance effectively lives as long as the singleton
With scope validation on (default in Development) resolving it throws InvalidOperationException
Registering the dependency as transient makes it per-request inside the singleton
The scoped instance is recreated on every request even though the singleton exists
hint: The singleton is built only once.
explanation: The singleton's constructor runs once, so it captures one scoped instance for its whole lifetime (a captive dependency); validation detects this. A transient injected into a singleton is also resolved once and kept.

text: Which statements about disposal in the built-in DI container are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Services created in a request scope are disposed when that scope is disposed
Instances passed in via AddSingleton(instance) are not disposed by the container
A transient IDisposable resolved from the root provider is held until the root provider is disposed
The container disposes transient instances immediately after each use
hint: The container disposes only what it created and tracks it.
explanation: The container tracks disposable instances it creates and disposes them with their owning scope or root, which makes root-resolved transients a leak risk. It does not own instances you supply. It never disposes transients right after use.

text: Given these registrations, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: GetRequiredService<IFoo>() returns an A
GetServices<IFoo>() enumerates A then B
GetRequiredService<IFoo>() returns a B
GetRequiredService<IFoo>() throws an ambiguity exception
hint: The last registration wins for single resolution.
explanation: For a single service the last registration wins, while IEnumerable<IFoo> contains all registrations in registration order. The container never throws for multiple registrations of the same service type.
code:
services.AddTransient<IFoo, A>();
services.AddTransient<IFoo, B>();

text: A BackgroundService needs to use a scoped DbContext each time it processes a message. What is the correct approach?
options: Resolve the DbContext from the root IServiceProvider and keep it
Inject the DbContext in the constructor of the BackgroundService
Register the BackgroundService as scoped
Inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work
hint: Hosted services are singletons.
explanation: Hosted services live for the app lifetime, so injecting a scoped service captures it forever. Creating a scope per unit of work gives a fresh DbContext that is disposed afterward. Resolving scoped services from the root provider is invalid or leaky.

text: What is returned by this code?
options: An instance of A
An instance of B
An InvalidOperationException because IFoo is registered twice
null
hint: TryAdd checks for an existing registration.
explanation: TryAddSingleton registers only when no registration for the service type already exists, so the earlier AddSingleton wins. B is never registered.

text: Which statements about middleware ordering are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Static files middleware must always come after endpoint mapping
UseAuthentication must be registered before UseAuthorization
UseAuthorization must be registered before UseAuthentication
UseExceptionHandler should be registered early so it can catch exceptions from later middleware
hint: Authorization needs an identity to evaluate.
explanation: Authorization relies on the user established by authentication, so authentication goes first. An exception handler only sees exceptions from middleware that runs after it. Static files typically come early and short-circuit.

text: What is the response body of a request?
options: BAC
ABC
ACB
AB
hint: Code after next() runs after later middleware complete.
explanation: The first middleware writes A, awaits next which runs the terminal middleware writing B, and then writes C once control returns. The pipeline unwinds in reverse order, so the sequence is ABC.

text: app.UseExceptionHandler("/error") is called after a terminal app.Run(ctx => throw new Exception()). What happens when a request is made?
options: The request returns 404
The exception handler catches it because it is registered
The exception propagates to the server because the handler is never reached in the pipeline
The handler runs only in the Development environment
hint: A terminal middleware never calls next.
explanation: Middleware is a chain in registration order and an exception handler only catches exceptions thrown by components after it. Since app.Run is terminal and comes first, the later handler is never part of the executed path.

text: Which statements about this middleware are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Setting the header throws InvalidOperationException because the response has already started
Headers are buffered until the middleware returns so the header is sent
The header is silently ignored without any exception
ctx.Response.HasStarted is true after the WriteAsync completes
hint: Headers must be sent before the body.
explanation: Once the body begins to flush, headers are sent and become read-only, so modifying them throws and HasStarted is true. Kestrel does not buffer headers until the middleware ends.

text: In a controller annotated with [ApiController], which statements about parameter binding and validation are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Complex type parameters are inferred as [FromForm]
Automatic HTTP 400 for invalid ModelState happens after the action body runs
A simple-type parameter that is not in the route template is inferred as [FromQuery]
A complex type parameter is inferred as [FromBody]
hint: Binding source inference rules.
explanation: ApiController infers FromBody for complex types and Route or Query for simple ones. Its validation filter short-circuits with 400 before the action executes. FromForm is inferred only for IFormFile types.

text: With <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in a project using [ApiController], what happens when a POST body {} is bound to this DTO?
options: A 500 NullReferenceException is thrown
Name is set to an empty string
Name is null and the action runs normally
A 400 response is returned automatically because non-nullable reference type properties are treated as [Required]
hint: Nullable annotations influence validation metadata.
explanation: MVC treats non-nullable reference type properties as implicitly required, so the missing Name makes ModelState invalid and ApiController returns 400. This is by default and can be disabled.

text: A singleton service must observe configuration values that change at runtime (reloadOnChange). Which type should it inject?
options: IOptionsMonitor<T>
T directly via AddSingleton(T)
IOptions<T>
IOptionsSnapshot<T>
hint: One option type is registered as singleton and supports change notifications.
explanation: IOptionsMonitor<T> is a singleton that always returns current values and offers OnChange. IOptions<T> is computed once, and IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped, so it cannot be injected into a singleton.

text: Why is creating a new HttpClient per request inside a using block discouraged in a long-running service?
options: HttpClient is not thread-safe
It can exhaust sockets because disposed connections linger in TIME_WAIT, and the pool is not reused
HttpClient cannot be disposed
Each HttpClient allocates a new thread
hint: Think about connections, not threads.
explanation: Each HttpClient with its own handler opens its own connections, which remain in TIME_WAIT after disposal and can exhaust sockets. HttpClient is safe for concurrent use, and IHttpClientFactory or a long-lived instance reuses the connection pool.

text: Which of these declarations compile? (Select all that apply.)
options: List<object> b = new List<string>();
IEnumerable<object> a = new List<string>();
IList<object> d = new List<string>();
Action<string> c = new Action<object>(o => { });
hint: Only some interfaces/delegates have in or out type parameters.
explanation: IEnumerable<out T> is covariant and Action<in T> is contravariant. List<T> is a class, and IList<T> is invariant because it both reads and writes T.

text: What happens at runtime?
options: It does not compile
It runs and stores 42 in arr[1]
ArrayTypeMismatchException on the last line
InvalidCastException on the first line
hint: Array covariance is checked at runtime.
explanation: string[] converts to object[] due to array covariance, but the runtime still verifies each store against the real element type. Storing an int throws ArrayTypeMismatchException.

text: Why does 'IEnumerable<object> e = new List<int>();' fail to compile?
options: List<int> does not implement IEnumerable
object cannot be used as a type argument
IEnumerable<T> is invariant
Variance only applies to reference-type arguments; int needs a boxing conversion, not a reference conversion
hint: Variance requires an identity or reference conversion.
explanation: Generic variance is allowed only when the type arguments are related by identity or reference conversion; int to object is a boxing conversion. IEnumerable<T> is covariant and List<int> does implement it.

text: Static counters on a generic class are incremented through different type arguments. What is printed?
hint: Each closed generic type gets its own statics.
explanation: Static fields are per constructed type, so C<int> and C<string> have separate Count fields. C<int>.Count is incremented twice and C<string>.Count once.

text: What happens when the code assigns to a member of a struct element obtained through a List indexer?
options: It sets X to 5
Compile error CS1612: cannot modify the return value because it is not a variable
InvalidOperationException at runtime
It sets X on a copy and silently does nothing
hint: What does the List indexer return for a struct element?
explanation: The indexer returns a copy of the struct, so assigning to a member of that temporary is rejected by the compiler. Replace the element with a modified copy, or use CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan with ref access.

text: A mutating method is called on a readonly field holding a struct. What is printed?
options: It does not compile
It throws
hint: Calling a method on a readonly field of struct type.
explanation: Because the field is readonly, the call Inc() operates on a defensive copy of the struct, so the original N remains 0. Making Counter a readonly struct or the field non-readonly changes this.

text: An int is boxed and the original variable is changed afterwards. What is printed after unboxing?
options: It does not compile
It throws InvalidCastException
hint: Boxing copies the value.
explanation: Boxing copies the int to the heap, so later changes to i do not affect the box. Unboxing yields the copied 5.

text: What does this code do?
options: Throws InvalidCastException because unboxing requires the exact original type
Prints 5 because int converts implicitly to long
Does not compile
Prints 5
hint: Unboxing must match the boxed type.
explanation: Unboxing is only allowed to the exact boxed type (or its nullable), so unboxing an int box as long throws. You need (long)(int)o instead.

text: Which of these cause a boxing allocation? (Select all that apply.)
options: int i = 3; string s = i.ToString();
string.Format("{0}", 5)
list.Add(1) where list is List<int>
object o = 3;
hint: Where is a value type converted to object?
explanation: The int is boxed to be passed in the object[] params array and assigned to object. List<int>.Add is generic over int, and int.ToString is called directly on the value without boxing.

text: Two object-typed references hold equal string contents. What do == and Equals report?
options: True True
False True
True False
False False
hint: == on two object-typed expressions is reference equality.
explanation: With both operands typed as object, == compares references, and the two strings are different instances. Equals is virtual and string overrides it for value comparison.

text: Comparing string references: a literal, a constant concatenation and a runtime concatenation. What is printed?
options: False False
True True
True False
False True
hint: Compile-time constants are interned; runtime concatenations are not.
explanation: 'hel' + 'lo' is folded to the literal 'hello' by the compiler, so it's the same interned reference. The runtime concatenation creates a new string instance, so ReferenceEquals is false.

text: Two positional records hold different List<int> instances with the same contents. What does == print?
options: It does not compile
It throws
True
False
hint: How does a record compare its members?
explanation: The synthesized record equality compares each property with EqualityComparer<T>.Default, and List<int> uses reference equality. The two lists are different instances, so the records are not equal.

text: Which statements about records are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A with-expression on a record class creates a shallow copy
== on a record class compares members by value using the synthesized equality
Positional properties of a record struct are init-only like a record class
Records are always value types
hint: Compare record class and record struct defaults.
explanation: A with-expression copies the object and reference-type members are shared, and the synthesized operator == compares members. Records may be classes or structs, and positional record struct properties are mutable by default.

text: What happens when a Span<int> local is used after an await in an async method?
options: It does not compile: a ref struct (Span<int>) cannot be used across an await
It throws at runtime
It compiles but s becomes empty after the await
It compiles and runs
hint: Async state machines are heap-allocated classes/structs.
explanation: A ref struct must live on the stack, but locals that span an await are hoisted into the state machine. The compiler rejects using the Span after the await. Using it before the await only, or Memory<T>, is fine.

text: A span slice and a range-sliced array are each modified. What is printed?
hint: One slice shares memory and the other copies.
explanation: AsSpan creates a view into the same array so s[0] = 99 changes a[1]. The range a[1..3] on an array copies the elements, so changing b does not affect a.

text: A ref local is taken to an array element and the array variable is then reassigned. What is printed?
hint: A ref local aliases a specific storage location.
explanation: The ref local points at the first element of the original array, and reassigning arr does not retarget it. Writing through r modifies the old array while arr[0] reads from the new one.

text: Which are poor choices as a lock target? (Select all that apply.)
options: lock (this)
lock (_gate) where _gate is a private readonly object
lock (typeof(Foo))
lock ("gate")
hint: Outside code can reach these objects too.
explanation: Publicly reachable objects such as this, Type objects and interned string literals can be locked by unrelated code, creating deadlocks. A private dedicated object cannot.

text: Which approaches make this counter update thread-safe? (Select all that apply.)
options: lock (_gate) { counter++; }
Interlocked.Increment(ref counter)
Declaring the field volatile and using counter++
Making the field static
hint: Read-modify-write needs to be atomic.
explanation: Interlocked and lock make the read-modify-write atomic. volatile gives visibility and ordering guarantees only, and static says nothing about atomicity.

text: Which statements about ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, valueFactory) are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The valueFactory can be invoked more than once for the same key under contention
Only one value is stored, and all callers get the stored one
The valueFactory is executed while holding the dictionary's lock
The valueFactory is guaranteed to run exactly once per key
hint: The factory is invoked outside of the internal locks.
explanation: Competing threads may each run the factory, but only one result wins and is returned to everyone. The factory runs outside the lock, so it needs to be side-effect free. Wrap values in Lazy<T> for single execution.

text: Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: lock (Monitor) is reentrant for the same thread
SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync can be used to guard async critical sections
Using await inside a lock statement body is a compile-time error
SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is reentrant for the same thread
hint: Locks are tied to thread ownership.
explanation: A lock body can't contain await because the continuation might resume on another thread, so use SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync. Monitor-based lock is reentrant but SemaphoreSlim is not, so recursive waits would deadlock.

text: An AsyncLocal value is changed inside Task.Run. What does the caller read afterwards?
options: It throws
hint: AsyncLocal values flow downwards via ExecutionContext copies.
explanation: Task.Run captures a copy of the ExecutionContext, so changes made inside the child do not flow back to the caller. The parent still sees 1.

text: What is the main effect of giving a class a finalizer on its garbage collection?
options: Instances survive at least one extra GC because they must be queued for finalization first
The finalizer runs immediately when the last reference is dropped
Instances are allocated on the LOH
Instances are collected faster
hint: The GC cannot reclaim the memory until the finalizer has run.
explanation: Finalizable objects are registered, and when found unreachable they are promoted to the f-reachable queue to run their finalizer, delaying reclamation. GC.SuppressFinalize in Dispose removes this cost. Finalizers do not run immediately.

text: A short-lived view model subscribes to a static event with 'Publisher.Changed += OnChanged;' and never unsubscribes. What is the effect?
options: Nothing; the GC ignores event subscriptions
The view model stays reachable via the static event's delegate list, causing a memory leak
The subscription is automatically removed when the view model goes out of scope
The event raises ObjectDisposedException
hint: Who holds a reference to whom?
explanation: The delegate stored in the static event references the view model instance, keeping it reachable from a GC root. Unsubscribe or use weak events.

text: Which statements about the Large Object Heap (LOH) are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Objects of 85,000 bytes or more are allocated on the LOH
The LOH is compacted on every collection by default
The LOH is collected only as part of a generation 2 collection
LOH objects start in generation 0 and are promoted
hint: Large objects are treated as part of gen 2.
explanation: Large objects go to the LOH, which is logically part of gen 2 so it is collected only with a full GC. It is not compacted by default and objects are not allocated in gen 0.

text: Two using declarations appear in a method body. In what order is output produced?
options: b a body
body a b
body b a
a b body
hint: Using declarations dispose at the end of the enclosing scope in reverse order.
explanation: A using declaration disposes at the end of the enclosing scope, so the body runs first. Disposal is in reverse order of declaration, b before a.

text: Which statements about finalizers are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The order in which finalizers run across objects is not guaranteed
They are not guaranteed to run when the process exits in .NET Core
They run on the thread that dropped the last reference
They run immediately when the object becomes unreachable
hint: A dedicated thread runs finalizers.
explanation: Finalizers run on a dedicated finalizer thread at an unspecified time, with no ordering guarantee, and .NET Core does not run them at shutdown. They are not immediate.

text: A switch expression with guarded type, property and null patterns is called with four values. What is printed?
options: big,int,empty,other
int,int,empty,null
big,int,empty, followed by an exception
big,int,empty,null
hint: Arms are evaluated top to bottom.
explanation: 11 matches the guarded int arm, 7 falls to the plain int arm, the empty string matches the property pattern, and null matches the null pattern since a type pattern never matches null.

text: What is the behavior of N(Color.Blue)?
options: Throws SwitchExpressionException at runtime, with a compiler warning for non-exhaustiveness
Compile error
Returns null
Returns an empty string
hint: Switch expressions must produce a value.
explanation: Missing enum cases produce warning CS8509, and when no arm matches at runtime a SwitchExpressionException is thrown. It is not a compile error and no default value is produced.

text: For int[] a = { 1, 2, 3 }, which expressions evaluate to true? (Select all that apply.)
hint: A slice pattern can match zero elements.
explanation: [1, .., 3] matches first and last, and [1, 2, 3, ..] matches with an empty slice. [_, _] requires exactly two elements and [.., 2] requires the last element to be 2.

text: A class overloads == to always return true. What do 'p == null' and 'p is null' print?
options: True True
True False
False True
False False
hint: Constant patterns do not call user-defined operators.
explanation: p == null calls the overloaded operator, which always returns true here. 'is null' performs a direct null check and bypasses operator overloading, so it is false.

text: A captured local used in a Where predicate is changed before the query is enumerated. What is printed?
hint: The lambda reads the captured variable when enumerated.
explanation: The lambda captures the variable threshold, and the query only runs at ToList, after threshold is 3. Only 4 is greater than 3.

text: Words are sorted by length with OrderBy. What order is printed?
options: bb cc a d
d a bb cc
a d cc bb
a d bb cc
hint: LINQ OrderBy is a stable sort.
explanation: OrderBy is stable, so elements with equal keys keep their original relative order: a before d, and bb before cc. An unstable sort like Array.Sort could reorder ties.
code:
var words = new[] { "bb", "a", "cc", "d" };
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", words.OrderBy(w => w.Length)));

text: Which statements are correct about rethrowing exceptions? (Select all that apply.)
options: 'throw ex;' preserves the original stack trace
'throw ex;' resets the stack trace to the point of the rethrow
'throw;' preserves the original stack trace
ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw() preserves the original stack trace
hint: Only the bare form keeps the origin.
explanation: A bare throw rethrows without altering the trace, and ExceptionDispatchInfo does the same from outside a catch. 'throw ex;' restarts the stack trace at that statement.

text: An exception filter, an inner finally and a catch all participate in one throw. What is the output order?
options: filter finally catch
catch filter finally
filter catch finally
finally filter catch
hint: Exception filters run during the first pass, before unwinding.
explanation: The runtime evaluates filters in a first pass before any finally block runs, then unwinds, running the inner finally, and finally enters the catch. So the output is 'filter finally catch'.

text: A static field initializer throws, and the field is read twice in separate try blocks. What is printed?
options: Exception then Exception
TypeInitializationException then TypeInitializationException
Exception then TypeInitializationException
TypeInitializationException then Exception
hint: A failed type initializer leaves the type unusable.
explanation: A static initializer failure is wrapped in TypeInitializationException, and the type remains permanently in a failed state, so later accesses throw it again.

text: Which statement about the Large Object Heap (LOH) in the .NET GC is correct?
options: Objects of 85,000 bytes or more are allocated on the LOH, which is collected only with gen 0 collections
The LOH is always compacted on every gen 1 collection
Objects of roughly 85,000 bytes or more are allocated on the LOH, which is logically collected together with gen 2
Only arrays can ever be allocated on the LOH; strings never are
hint: Think about the size threshold and which generation the LOH is tied to.
explanation: Large objects (about 85,000 bytes and up) go to the LOH, which is collected as part of gen 2 collections and is not compacted by default. Gen 0 and gen 1 collections do not touch it. Strings can also land on the LOH when large enough.

text: Which statements about server GC versus workstation GC are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Server GC never compacts the heap
Server GC generally favors throughput at the cost of higher memory use
Server GC creates a separate heap and dedicated GC thread per logical core
Workstation GC cannot perform background (concurrent) gen 2 collections
hint: Server GC trades memory for parallel throughput.
explanation: Server GC uses per-core heaps and GC threads and is tuned for throughput, so it uses more memory. Workstation GC does support background GC, and both flavors can compact.

text: Which statements about Span<T> are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It cannot be captured by a lambda or stored in a closure
It cannot be a field of a class or be boxed because it is a ref struct
It cannot wrap an existing managed array, only stack memory
Slicing it with Slice() copies the elements into a new buffer
It can wrap memory obtained from stackalloc in safe code
hint: Span<T> must live on the stack.
explanation: As a ref struct, Span<T> is restricted to the stack: no boxing, no class fields, no closure capture. It can wrap arrays and stackalloc memory, and Slice returns a view over the same memory without copying.

text: Which statements about consuming a ValueTask<T> are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A ValueTask<T> always avoids heap allocation
Task.WhenAll accepts ValueTask<T> instances directly without conversion
Call AsTask() if you need to await it more than once or store it for later use
It must not be awaited multiple times
hint: A ValueTask may wrap a pooled, reusable source.
explanation: A ValueTask can wrap an IValueTaskSource that is reused, so it is single-consumption; AsTask gives a safely shareable Task. It only avoids allocation when it completes synchronously or is backed by a pooled source, and WhenAll requires Tasks.

text: In the snippet, what happens when F() is called without awaiting it?
options: The call returns a faulted Task and the exception is observed when the Task is awaited or inspected
The exception is thrown synchronously from the call to F()
The exception is swallowed permanently and can never be observed
The process crashes immediately because the exception is unhandled
hint: The async state machine catches exceptions and stores them in the returned Task.
explanation: The compiler-generated state machine wraps the body in try/catch and sets the exception on the AsyncTaskMethodBuilder's Task. The caller therefore gets a faulted Task, and the exception only surfaces on await, Wait or Result. It is not thrown synchronously.

text: In an ASP.NET Core application, which statement about ConfigureAwait(false) and blocking calls is most accurate?
options: Omitting ConfigureAwait(false) will classically deadlock on .Result, exactly like in ASP.NET Framework
ConfigureAwait(false) makes the awaited operation run on a new dedicated thread
ConfigureAwait(false) prevents the state machine from being generated
ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so the classic context deadlock does not occur, but sync-over-async can still cause thread pool starvation
hint: Think about what ASP.NET Core removed compared to ASP.NET Framework.
explanation: ASP.NET Core does not install a request SynchronizationContext, so the classic deadlock is gone. Blocking on async code still ties up thread pool threads and can starve the pool. ConfigureAwait(false) only controls context capture for continuations.

text: What does the following code print?
options: It throws because AsyncLocal cannot be set inside an async method
hint: Changes made to an ambient value inside an async callee are not visible to the caller after it returns.
