explanation: ExecutionContext flows down into async calls, but modifications made inside the callee's async method apply to its own copy and are undone when control returns to the caller. The caller still sees 1. AsyncLocal can be set anywhere.

text: Given a bounded channel created with FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait that is currently full, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The ValueTask returned by writer.WriteAsync(item) completes once space becomes available
With BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite, WriteAsync completes successfully but the item is discarded
writer.TryWrite(item) returns false
writer.WriteAsync(item) throws ChannelClosedException immediately
hint: Distinguish Wait mode from the drop modes.
explanation: In Wait mode TryWrite fails and WriteAsync asynchronously waits for room. DropWrite silently discards the item being written. A ChannelClosedException is only thrown if the writer was completed.

text: When does ChannelReader<T>.Completion complete normally?
options: As soon as the writer calls Complete(), even if items are still buffered
When the channel's buffer first becomes empty
After the writer has called Complete() and all buffered items have been read
Only when the reader's CancellationToken is cancelled
hint: Completion represents the end of data, not just the end of writing.
explanation: Completion finishes only after the writer is marked complete and the buffer has been drained, which is what lets ReadAllAsync terminate cleanly. Completing the writer alone is not enough while items remain.

text: Why does C# forbid await inside a lock statement, and what is the usual alternative?
options: Monitor is owned by a thread, and the continuation may resume on a different thread; use SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with WaitAsync instead
await is forbidden because the lock keyword compiles to a spin lock; use Thread.Sleep instead
The compiler cannot generate a state machine inside try/finally; use a nested method
It is allowed but only in static methods; use a static lock object
hint: Monitor ownership is tied to a managed thread id.
explanation: Monitor.Exit must be called by the owning thread, but after an await the code may resume on another thread, so the compiler reports an error. SemaphoreSlim is not thread-affine and supports WaitAsync. Async methods can contain try/finally.

text: In this method, what is the bug and the correct fix?
options: No bug: Release is always correct in finally
WaitAsync must be called with ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid releasing twice
SemaphoreSlim cannot be used with CancellationToken, so remove the token
If WaitAsync(ct) throws OperationCanceledException, finally still calls Release and inflates the count; move WaitAsync before the try block
hint: Release should only happen if the wait succeeded.
explanation: When WaitAsync is inside the try and is cancelled, the semaphore was never acquired, yet finally releases it, permanently increasing the available count and breaking mutual exclusion. Acquire before entering try so finally runs only after a successful acquire.

text: Which statements about lock-free updates with Interlocked are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Interlocked.Increment performs an atomic read-modify-write
Interlocked.Read is required to read an int safely on 64-bit platforms
Interlocked.CompareExchange in a retry loop can implement arbitrary atomic read-modify-write updates
Writing count = count + 1 on a volatile int is atomic
hint: volatile gives ordering, not atomic read-modify-write.
explanation: Interlocked.Increment is atomic, and a CompareExchange loop can build other atomic updates. A volatile read followed by a write is two separate operations, so increments can be lost. Interlocked.Read is only relevant for 64-bit values on 32-bit platforms.

text: What does marking a field volatile guarantee in the .NET memory model?
options: It makes compound operations like i++ atomic
Reads have acquire semantics and writes have release semantics, but compound operations are not atomic
It forces the field to be allocated on the stack
It gives a full fence around every access, equivalent to a lock
hint: Think acquire/release, not atomicity.
explanation: Volatile reads are acquire and volatile writes are release, limiting reordering around them. It does not make read-modify-write atomic and is not a full fence or a lock.

text: Which statements about expression trees are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: An Expression<Func<T,bool>> can be inspected by a provider such as EF Core and translated to SQL
C# lets you convert a lambda with a statement body to Expression<Func<T>> without restriction
Expression trees are immutable, so changes are made by rewriting with an ExpressionVisitor
Calling Compile() repeatedly is cheap, so caching the delegate is unnecessary
hint: Think data-as-code, and what the compiler allows in expression lambdas.
explanation: Expression trees describe code as data and are immutable, so ExpressionVisitor builds modified copies. Compile() emits IL and is expensive, so delegates should be cached. The compiler rejects statement lambdas for expression trees.

text: For the lambda below, how is the captured local id represented in the expression tree?
options: As a ConstantExpression holding the int 5 evaluated at compile time
As a ParameterExpression named id
As a MemberExpression reading a field of a compiler-generated closure object held in a ConstantExpression
As a MethodCallExpression to Convert.ToInt32
hint: Captured variables live in a closure class.
explanation: The compiler hoists captured locals into a closure class instance, and the tree contains a field access on a constant of that closure type. That is why providers like EF Core can parameterize it and re-evaluate on each execution. It is not folded to a constant of 5.

text: Which statements about Roslyn source generators are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: They can rewrite the bodies of existing methods in user files
They can call into the compiled output of the project they are generating code for
They can add new source files to a compilation but cannot modify existing user code
IIncrementalGenerator is preferred over ISourceGenerator because it caches pipeline stages
hint: Generators are additive and run inside the compiler.
explanation: Generators only add code, and incremental generators cache stage results to keep the IDE responsive. They run before the target assembly exists, so they cannot call its compiled output or rewrite existing code.

text: In an IIncrementalGenerator pipeline, what is the key practice for good caching and IDE performance?
options: Transform syntax early into small value-equatable models (such as records) and avoid carrying ISymbol or Compilation objects downstream
Store the full Compilation in each pipeline step so results are always fresh
Use static mutable dictionaries to cache models across runs
Perform all work in the final RegisterSourceOutput step using SyntaxNode trees
hint: Incremental stages are skipped only when their inputs compare equal.
explanation: The pipeline reuses cached outputs when a stage's input is equal to the previous one, so models need value equality, and symbols or compilations change on nearly every edit and defeat caching. Static mutable caches are unsafe and unnecessary.

text: Which statements about EF Core tracking are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A no-tracking query returns the same instance for repeated rows with the same key
A context can track two different instances with the same primary key at the same time
For tracked entities, DetectChanges compares current property values against a snapshot
AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution returns a single instance per key within the query results
hint: Identity resolution is what the tracker normally provides.
explanation: The default tracker uses snapshots and enforces one instance per key. Plain no-tracking queries may materialize separate instances for repeated rows, which AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution fixes within a query. Tracking two instances with the same key throws.

text: How does EF Core optimistic concurrency with a configured concurrency token work? (Select all that apply.)
options: The UPDATE or DELETE includes the original token value in its WHERE clause
A DbUpdateConcurrencyException is thrown when the affected row count is not the expected one
It takes a pessimistic lock on the row when the entity is loaded
The token value used is re-read from the database at SaveChanges time
hint: The original values come from when the entity was loaded.
explanation: EF adds the original token value to the WHERE clause and treats an unexpected affected-row count as a conflict. No row lock is taken, and the original value comes from load time, which is the point of the check.

text: Which statements about AsSplitQuery in EF Core are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It requires AsNoTracking to work
It uses multiple round trips, and data can change between them unless a suitable transaction isolation is used
It guarantees a consistent snapshot across all the generated SQL queries
It avoids cartesian explosion when including multiple collection navigations
hint: Multiple queries means multiple points in time.
explanation: Split queries issue separate SQL statements per collection to avoid duplicated parent rows. Without a snapshot or serializable transaction, results may be inconsistent between the statements. It works with tracking queries.
code:
var blogs = await db.Blogs
    .Include(b => b.Posts)
    .Include(b => b.Tags)
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .ToListAsync();

text: What is the main benefit of EF.CompileAsyncQuery?
options: It caches the result rows in memory between calls
It turns the query into a stored procedure on the database
It disables parameterization to reuse database plans
The query is translated once and reused through a delegate, skipping per-call query cache lookup and preprocessing
hint: It optimizes the client-side pipeline, not the database.
explanation: A compiled query keeps the translated query in a delegate, removing repeated expression processing and cache-key computation. It does not cache data, create stored procedures, or change parameterization.

text: What is true about ExecuteUpdateAsync in EF Core?
options: It loads the entities into the change tracker, modifies them, then calls SaveChanges
It runs a set-based UPDATE directly in the database, and already tracked entities are not refreshed
It only works inside a SaveChanges transaction
It raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException automatically for rowversion columns
hint: It bypasses the change tracker entirely.
explanation: ExecuteUpdate translates to a single UPDATE statement without materializing entities, so tracked instances can become stale. It does not use the tracker or concurrency token checks.

text: Which statements about the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: app.Run adds a terminal middleware that has no next delegate
Response processing runs through middleware in the same order as request processing
A middleware that does not call next short-circuits the pipeline
Exception handling middleware registered first can catch exceptions thrown by middleware registered after it
hint: Think of the pipeline as nested calls.
explanation: Middleware are nested delegates: skipping next short-circuits, and an outer try/catch sees exceptions from inner components. Run is terminal. The response travels back through the middleware in reverse order.

text: An exception is thrown after the response body has already started streaming. What can an exception-handling middleware do?
options: Change the status code to 500 as usual
Clear the already-sent headers with Response.Clear()
Nothing useful to the status code; once HasStarted is true headers are sent, so it can only abort the connection or log
Restart the request pipeline from the beginning
hint: Headers go out before the body.
explanation: After the first body bytes are flushed, status and headers are already on the wire and cannot be modified. Handlers should check Response.HasStarted and typically log and abort. Clear fails or is ignored once the response has started.

text: What is a known characteristic of the fixed window rate limiter compared to a sliding window?
options: Up to about twice the permit limit can pass in a short period that straddles a window boundary
It never allows more than the limit in any time span
It cannot be partitioned per user
It queues requests by default with unlimited queue length
hint: Think of requests at the end of one window and the start of the next.
explanation: A fixed window resets counts at boundaries, so bursts at the end of one window and the start of the next can approach twice the limit. Sliding windows smooth this. Fixed window limiters can be partitioned and do not queue unboundedly by default.

text: Which statements about ASP.NET Core output caching are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: By default only 200 responses to GET or HEAD requests are cached
By default it does not honor a client's Cache-Control: no-cache request header the way response caching does
Cache entries can be evicted by tag using IOutputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync
Responses are stored in the client browser cache
hint: Output caching is server-side and policy-driven.
explanation: Output caching stores responses on the server, supports tag-based eviction, and is controlled by server policies rather than client headers. The default policy caches only 200 GET/HEAD responses. Browser storage is a different feature.

text: What is the recommended design for liveness versus readiness health checks in an orchestrated environment?
options: Liveness should check all downstream dependencies so unhealthy pods restart
Both probes should run the same checks to avoid confusion
Readiness should return 200 always so traffic is never interrupted
Liveness should be cheap and reflect only whether the process itself is healthy, while readiness checks dependencies and ability to serve traffic
hint: A restart should not be triggered by an external outage.
explanation: A liveness probe that depends on a database can restart every instance during a database outage, making things worse. Readiness gates traffic and may check dependencies. Typically these are mapped as separate health check endpoints using tags.

text: In the snippet, how does an endpoint filter reject invalid input without invoking the handler?
options: Throw OperationCanceledException
Return an IResult without calling next(context)
Set context.HttpContext.Response.HasStarted to true
Call next(context) twice
hint: A filter wraps the handler like middleware.
explanation: An IEndpointFilter chooses whether to call next. Returning a result directly short-circuits the handler and later filters. Throwing cancellation would not produce a proper validation response.

text: Which statements about dependency injection lifetimes in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: ServiceProviderOptions.ValidateScopes can detect resolving scoped services from the root provider
A singleton that takes a scoped service in its constructor creates a captive dependency
A singleton can create scopes on demand with IServiceScopeFactory to use scoped services safely
Transient IDisposable services are never disposed by the container
hint: The container tracks disposables it creates.
explanation: Capturing a scoped service in a singleton keeps it alive for the app lifetime. ValidateScopes and scope factories address that. The container does track and dispose transient disposables it creates, at the end of their scope.

text: Given the registration below, what happens when you call provider.GetRequiredService<ICache>() with no key?
options: It returns the RedisCache because it is the only ICache registered
It returns the first keyed registration alphabetically
It returns null
It throws InvalidOperationException because keyed registrations are not resolved by a non-keyed request
hint: Keyed and non-keyed registrations are looked up separately.
explanation: A keyed registration only matches requests that supply a matching key, such as [FromKeyedServices("redis")] or GetRequiredKeyedService. A non-keyed request finds no registration and GetRequiredService throws.
code:
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<ICache, RedisCache>("redis");

public class Svc([FromKeyedServices("redis")] ICache cache) { }

text: Which services does the built-in DI container dispose when the provider or scope is disposed?
options: Only instances it created itself via a type or factory registration; instances registered with AddSingleton(instance) are not disposed by it
All services including pre-created instances registered with AddSingleton(instance)
Only scoped services, never singletons
None; services must always be disposed manually
hint: Ownership matters.
explanation: The container owns and disposes instances it creates, but caller-provided instances remain the caller's responsibility. Singletons created by the container are disposed when the root provider is disposed.

text: Which statements about the transactional outbox pattern are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Consumers should be idempotent because a relay can publish a message and crash before marking it sent
Publishing to the broker inside the transaction before committing makes it equivalent
A background relay reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them
The outbox row is inserted in the same database transaction as the business change
It gives exactly-once delivery to the broker without consumer cooperation
hint: The pattern gives at-least-once delivery.
explanation: The outbox atomically records intent with the state change, and a relay publishes later, which yields at-least-once delivery with possible duplicates. Publishing before commit can send messages for rolled-back changes, so it is not equivalent.

text: What is the most robust way to implement idempotency keys for a payment API?
options: Check a cache for the key, then process, with no locking
Rely on clients never retrying
Use the request timestamp as the key
Insert the key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effects, and return the stored response on replay
hint: A check-then-act race needs an atomic guard.
explanation: A unique constraint makes the claim atomic, and committing it together with the side effects avoids processing twice or losing the record. A non-atomic check allows concurrent duplicates. Timestamps do not identify retries.

text: Which statements about retry and circuit-breaker strategies are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retry storms
Infinite immediate retries are safe because they maximize success
An open circuit breaker fails calls fast, giving the dependency time to recover
Retrying a non-idempotent POST is safe without idempotency keys
hint: Retries amplify load on a failing dependency.
explanation: Jitter spreads retries and breakers shed load. Unbounded immediate retries can overload a struggling service, and retrying non-idempotent operations risks duplicate effects.

text: How does a Polly (v8) timeout strategy behave if the guarded delegate ignores its CancellationToken?
options: It aborts the thread running the delegate
It is cooperative: it signals cancellation through the token, so code that ignores the token keeps running
It throws ThreadAbortException into the delegate
It is guaranteed to terminate the underlying HTTP connection
hint: No thread is killed in modern .NET.
explanation: Timeouts rely on cancellation tokens, and nothing can forcibly stop code that does not observe them. Thread abort is not supported in .NET Core and later, and connection termination is not automatic.

text: Which approach makes JSON serialization compatible with Native AOT and trimming?
options: Use the default reflection-based serializer, which works unchanged
Disable the trimmer warnings
Use a source-generated JsonSerializerContext with JsonSerializable attributes
Use Type.GetType with strings to load converters
hint: Avoid runtime reflection over your types.
explanation: The source generator emits serialization metadata at compile time, so the trimmer and AOT compiler can see what is needed. Reflection-based serialization may fail when members are trimmed, and suppressing warnings only hides the problem.

text: Which statements about trimming and reflection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The trimmer cannot statically see types accessed only by string name through reflection and may remove them
PublishTrimmed removes only whole unused assemblies and never members
Type.GetType("Namespace.Type") is always safe with trimming
[DynamicallyAccessedMembers] annotations tell the trimmer which members must be preserved
hint: Static analysis cannot follow arbitrary strings.
explanation: The linker works on static reachability, so annotations or explicit roots are needed for reflection targets. Trimming removes unused types and members as well, so string-based lookup can break.

text: Which practices avoid common BenchmarkDotNet pitfalls? (Select all that apply.)
options: Running in Release without a debugger attached
Running benchmarks from a Debug build is fine for relative comparisons
Returning the computed result from the benchmark method so the JIT cannot eliminate the work as dead code
Building the input data inside the benchmark method because setup cost is excluded automatically
hint: Optimization and dead-code elimination affect measurements.
explanation: Release builds are required for meaningful JIT optimization, and returning or consuming results prevents dead-code elimination. Setup inside the benchmark body is measured, so it should be in [GlobalSetup] or [IterationSetup].
code:
[Benchmark]
public int Sum() => _data.Sum();   // result returned, not discarded

[GlobalSetup]
public void Setup() => _data = Enumerable.Range(0, 1000).ToArray();

text: On which thread do callbacks registered via CancellationToken.Register run when CancellationTokenSource.Cancel() is called?
options: Synchronously on the thread that calls Cancel(), by default
Always on a new thread pool thread
On the thread that created the token
On the thread that registered the callback
hint: Cancel() does not queue the callbacks.
explanation: Registered callbacks run inline on the thread that calls Cancel, so slow callbacks block the canceller. Use CancelAsync or move heavy work off the callback. They are not marshaled to the creating or registering thread.
